binders: A finite indexed family X1,…,XN of real random variables on a common probability space.
σ² defined as the sum of the individual variances.
hypotheses: For every i, |X_i-E X_i|≤K almost surely.
definitions_and_conventions: Each summand is centered by its expectation.
σ² is the sum of individual variances.
Probability and almost-sure statements use the common probability measure.
implicit_context: The variables are real-valued and the displayed expectations and variances exist and are finite.
The literal quotient presumes nonzero denominators although K>0 and σ²>0 are not stated.
If σ²=0, the centered sum is almost surely zero and every positive upper tail is null, but the printed formula requires a limiting or exceptional-case convention.

details: The variance scale is the sum of individual variances.
Independence identifies that sum with the centered sum's variance.
The same K bounds every |X_i-E X_i| almost surely.
The event is ∑(X_i-E X_i)≥t for t>0.
The inequality is one-sided and uses non-strict ≥.
The subsequent asymptotic regimes are commentary, not part of Theorem 2.9.2.

undebatable_constraints: The almost-sure bound applies to centered quantities and uses one common K.
The theorem applies for every t>0.
The event is the upper tail of the centered sum.
σ² is exactly the sum of individual variances.
No lower-tail or two-sided conclusion is printed.

contract_plain_english: For independent real random variables whose centered values are uniformly almost surely bounded by K, let σ² be the sum of their variances and h(u)=(1+u)log(1+u)-u. For every t>0, the probability that the centered sum is at least t is bounded by exp(-(σ²/K²)h(Kt/σ²)). The printed theorem is one-sided. Its displayed quotient has the usual nondegenerate interpretation K>0 and σ²>0; the zero-variance case requires an explicit exceptional-case or limiting convention.
